```plato
//==
// # Rigid dynamics
//
// The bodies for `rigid-dynamics.types.plato` and `rigid-dynamics.concepts.plato`:
// mass properties, the integrator, forces, and the sequential-impulse contact
// solver.
//
// Sections, in order:
//  - IForceModel2D and IForceModel3D — derived helpers
//  - Environmental force models — the ForceOn bodies
//  - Mass properties and inertia tensors
//  - Solver bodies — impulse response
//  - Forces, torques and impulses
//  - Integration
//  - The contact solver — one row
//  - The contact solver — passes and iteration
//  - The contact solver — position correction
//  - The step
//  - Array replacement
//  - Planar bodies
//
//== HOW THE SOLVER IS SHAPED, AND WHY
//
// Sequential impulses is an inherently sequential algorithm: it visits contacts
// one at a time and each visit reads velocities the previous visit wrote. That is
// Gauss-Seidel, and the sequencing is not incidental — it is the reason the method
// converges on a stack where a parallel (Jacobi) sweep of the same contacts
// oscillates. So the shape here is a FOLD:
//
//     one pass  = Reduce over the row indices, threading the whole world
//     the solve = Reduce over the iteration counter, threading the whole world
//
// The accumulator is the entire `RigidWorld3D`, not a velocity array, because a
// row visit writes THREE things: two body velocities and the row's own
// accumulated impulses. Threading the world makes the pass a total function of
// state with no aliasing question to answer, and makes `SolveRow` independently
// meaningful — it is "the world after solving this one contact once", which is
// exactly the unit a law test wants.
//
// WHAT THIS COSTS. Replacing one element of an immutable array rebuilds it, so a
// row visit is linear in the body count and a pass is rows times bodies. A
// mutable solver is rows times a constant. That is the price of the formulation
// and it is stated rather than hidden; it is also not the interesting term for
// the scene sizes this vocabulary is aimed at, where the row count dominates.
//
// WHAT WAS REJECTED.
//   * A JACOBI PASS — compute every row's impulse from one frozen velocity state,
//     then sum the contributions per body. It is a `Map` and a scatter, it
//     parallelizes, and its cost is the same product. It was rejected because it
//     does not converge on the case that matters: in a stack, each contact
//     computes the impulse needed to support the load ALONE, they all apply at
//     once, the stack is over-corrected, and the next iteration over-corrects
//     back. Under-relaxing fixes the oscillation and destroys the convergence
//     rate. Gauss-Seidel gets stacks right because contact n sees contact n-1's
//     work.
//   * A VELOCITY-ARRAY ACCUMULATOR with the impulses returned alongside. It saves
//     copying the settings through the fold and costs a second array to keep in
//     step with the first; the fold then has two things that must stay the same
//     length and one function that can violate it.
//   * BAUMGARTE BIAS INSIDE THE VELOCITY SOLVE — the usual textbook shortcut, in
//     which the penetration term is added to the target separation speed of the
//     ordinary velocity solve. It is one line and it is wrong in a way that shows:
//     the correction lands in the body's REAL velocity, so a body that starts
//     deeply overlapped is launched, and a resting stack visibly breathes as the
//     bias pumps energy in and damping takes it out. The correction here is a
//     separate pseudo-velocity pass (see "position correction") whose result moves
//     positions and is then thrown away, so no energy enters the simulation.

library RigidDynamics
{
    //==
    // # IForceModel2D and IForceModel3D — derived helpers
    //
    // An environmental force model yields the newton force on a body in its
    // current state via `ForceOn`; these derive that force's magnitude, the
    // acceleration it imparts (F = m a), and a negligibility test.

    // The magnitude of the force exerted on the body, in newtons.
    ForceMagnitudeOn(self: IForceModel2D, body: RigidBody2D): Number
        => self.ForceOn(body).Magnitude;

    // The acceleration this force imparts to the body: force over mass (F = m a),
    // in meters per second squared. Precondition: the body's mass is positive
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion).
    AccelerationOn(self: IForceModel2D, body: RigidBody2D): Vector2D
        => self.ForceOn(body) / body.MassProperties.Mass.Amount;

    // True when the force on the body is negligible, within the given
    // non-negative tolerance in newtons.
    IsNegligibleOn(self: IForceModel2D, body: RigidBody2D, tolerance: Number): Boolean
        => self.ForceOn(body).Magnitude <= tolerance;

    // The magnitude of the force exerted on the body, in newtons.
    ForceMagnitudeOn(self: IForceModel3D, body: RigidBody3D): Number
        => self.ForceOn(body).Magnitude;

    // The acceleration this force imparts to the body: force over mass (F = m a),
    // in meters per second squared. Precondition: the body's mass is positive.
    AccelerationOn(self: IForceModel3D, body: RigidBody3D): Vector3D
        => self.ForceOn(body) / body.MassProperties.Mass.Amount;

    // True when the force on the body is negligible, within the given
    // non-negative tolerance in newtons.
    IsNegligibleOn(self: IForceModel3D, body: RigidBody3D, tolerance: Number): Boolean
        => self.ForceOn(body).Magnitude <= tolerance;

    //==
    // # Environmental force models — the ForceOn bodies
    //
    // What each declared model actually exerts. Every one is a force in newtons on
    // the body as it currently stands, so a caller sums them and hands the total
    // to the integrator; none of them mutates or schedules anything.
    //
    // `BuoyancyModel` has no `ForceOn` here and does not claim `IForceModel3D`.
    // Buoyancy is minus the weight of the DISPLACED FLUID, and the displaced
    // volume is a shape query against the fluid half-space — a `RigidBody3D`
    // carries no shape, so the interface cannot supply the one number the force
    // depends on. `BuoyantForce` below takes that volume as an argument instead of
    // pretending to derive it.

    // Weight: the same acceleration on every body, scaled by its mass and its own
    // gravity multiplier. Static and kinematic bodies are not exempted here —
    // `SolverBody3D` exempts them by having no inverse mass, and a caller working
    // in `RigidBody3D` reads the motion kind through `MobilityScale`.
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity_of_Earth)
    ForceOn(self: UniformGravity2D, body: RigidBody2D): Vector2D
        => self.Acceleration * (body.MassProperties.Mass.Amount * body.GravityScale);

    // Weight under uniform gravity.
    ForceOn(self: UniformGravity3D, body: RigidBody3D): Vector3D
        => self.Acceleration * (body.MassProperties.Mass.Amount * body.GravityScale);

    // Newtonian attraction toward a point mass: magnitude mu * m / r^2, directed
    // from the body toward the centre. A body AT the centre has no direction to
    // fall in and feels nothing, which keeps the singularity out of the caller.
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_universal_gravitation)
    ForceOn(self: PointGravity, body: RigidBody3D): Vector3D
    {
        var toCentre = body.Pose.Position.Between(self.Center);
        var distanceSquared = toCentre.MagnitudeSquared;
        var magnitude = self.GravitationalParameter * body.MassProperties.Mass.Amount
            * body.GravityScale / distanceSquared;
        return distanceSquared <= 0.0 ? Vector3D.Zero : toCentre.Normalize * magnitude;
    }

    // Drag opposing motion: -(linear * v + quadratic * |v| * v). The linear term
    // dominates at low speed (Stokes) and the quadratic one at high speed
    // (form drag); carrying both lets one model cover the whole range.
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drag_(physics))
    ForceOn(self: DragModel, body: RigidBody3D): Vector3D
    {
        var v = body.LinearVelocity;
        return v.Negative * (self.LinearCoefficient + self.QuadraticCoefficient * v.Magnitude);
    }
```
